tier_reason: First-party README tables backed by public benchmark code (benches/alloc.rs, run via cargo bench with BENCH_FRESH=1 BENCH_SAFE_LIVE=1) and a named CPU (Ryzen 5 1600), but the rustc version, RUSTFLAGS, glibc version and the C/C++ flags used for the mimalloc/snmalloc comparators are not stated, so it falls short of A; no independent run exists.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Linux x86-64 (Ryzen 5 1600) direct-call table, ops/s: tight-small 1T 52.52 M/s vs glibc system 44.77, mimalloc 48.00, snmalloc 41.54 (1.09x vs best); mixed-small 8T 196.03 M/s vs system 37.17, mimalloc 40.42, snmalloc 57.87 (3.39x vs best); large-only 1T 7.36 M/s vs system 340 K/s, mimalloc 2.52 M/s (2.91x vs best); big-upper-tail 1T 6.28x vs best; zeroed-large 1T 86.63x vs best. README: '21/22 win-or-tie against the best comparator', but six of those wins are 1.02x-1.12x, inside the README's own ~10% noise floor, and one row (spawn-empty) is a pthread calibration row. Losses: zeroed-small 8T at 0.67x (allox 100.45 M/s vs snmalloc 148.91 M/s), and the process-global application benchmark (examples/app_workload.rs) at 4 threads, 250.8k vs mimalloc 268.1k and snmalloc 280.1k (0.94x and 0.90x); at 1 thread allox leads 1.06x. Windows table (no CPU named, talc/dlmalloc/system only, predates later work per README): 5/5 wins, 3.70x to 23.8x vs the system allocator.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo bench; the bench profile inherits [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1 from Cargo.toml; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated (MSRV 1.79). Comparators: mimalloc crate 0.1 and snmalloc-rs 0.7 (build_cc feature) compiled by their build scripts with unlogged C/C++ flags; 'system' is the distro glibc malloc (version unstated); talc 5 and dlmalloc 0.2 are Rust. Every allocator, allox included, is called through a &'static dyn GlobalAlloc, so allox gets no inlining advantage from LTO.
corrections.workload: 22 direct-call workloads in benches/alloc.rs driven through GlobalAlloc (small, mixed and large size classes at 1 and 8 threads, zeroed allocation, producer/consumer remote free, thread churn, a pthread calibration row, json-ish, request and ECS realloc-growth shapes); ops/s, higher is better. Each allocated block is written at one byte only, so the large and huge rows measure allocator bookkeeping and memory retention rather than memory traffic. A separate process-global String/Vec/HashMap application benchmark (examples/app_workload.rs, scripts/app_bench.sh) runs at 1 and 4 threads.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks; 1,355 commits, but the latest batch (2026-10-10/11) are docs-only commits that append hidden '<!-- updated: ... -->' comments to README.md; not published on crates.io (API: crate `allox` does not exist) despite the README's `allox = "0.1"` snippet.
corrections.caveats: Very young single-author repo (1 star), not on crates.io; commit count is inflated by README-comment padding commits. Workloads are the author's own and rows carry a stated ~10% noise floor (median of 3 x 2 s), so the 1.02x-1.12x 'wins' are ties. Each block is touched at one byte: large/huge rows reward allox for keeping arena memory mapped while glibc (mmap threshold) and snmalloc return or decommit it (snmalloc reads 1 K/s on huge-only), and zeroed-large 1T's 86.63x comes from skipping the memset of 5-8 MiB blocks after a madvise discard while the benchmark never faults in more than one page. README size-range labels disagree with the code (big-tail labelled 64K-256K is 262145-524289 in code; big-upper-tail 256K-1M is 524289-1048577; large-only 8T 32K-1M is 32768-262144). mimalloc/snmalloc measured through Rust GlobalAlloc wrappers with unlogged build flags, glibc version unstated, no independent reproduction. The README documents its losses (zeroed-small 8T, 4-thread app workload) and a known telemetry-counter defect rather than hiding them.
corrections.why_faster: README and benches/alloc.rs: per-thread lock-free free lists with byte-budgeted caches and sharded per-class heap locks touched only by batched slow paths; frameless fast paths; arena-backed big/large tiers that retain mapped memory and recycle it instead of unmapping (the main source of the large-row gaps against glibc and snmalloc); growable extents for realloc chains; virgin/discarded pages skip calloc memsets. These are allocator-design differences, not a Rust-versus-C codegen effect.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; confirm at C. Shortcomings to record: wins mostly within the stated 10% noise floor except mixed-size, medium and large rows; large-row gaps reflect memory retention under a one-byte-touch benchmark (zeroed-large 86.63x skips memset with one page touched); losses at zeroed-small 8T (0.67x) and the 4-thread application benchmark (0.90x-0.94x); repo is 1 star, unpublished on crates.io, with padding commits. same_opt_level left null: comparators are built by cc/cmake build scripts under the bench profile (likely -O3) and glibc is the distro build, but no build log states the flags.

tier_reason: First-party README hyperfine tables against pigz 2.4 with the CPU named (Ryzen 9 3950X) and a public benchmark.sh, but the rustc version of the run is not stated, pigz is an apt binary with unstated flags, and the README's command lines (-c level, stdin) come from an older revision of benchmark.sh than the one in the repo (-l level, file argument, extra mgzip rows), so it is not reproducible enough for A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --no-default-features --features deflate_rust,libdeflate,snap_default (benchmark.sh; default release profile, no [profile.release] overrides); rustc version for the original run not stated (repo now pins 1.97.1 in rust-toolchain.toml). The README tables use 'crabz -p N -c L < data.txt' while the current benchmark.sh runs 'crabz -p N -l L -f gzip ./data.txt', so the tables came from an earlier script revision. Every build, the deflate_rust one included, installs mimalloc (C) as #[global_allocator] (src/main.rs; also present in the v0.7.0 and v0.10.0 Cargo.toml). pigz is the Ubuntu 20 apt binary with unstated flags. hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 3. Decompression inputs are made by system gzip -3/-6/-9.
corrections.caveats: Not a like-for-like deflate comparison: the deflate_rust backend is miniz_oxide, whose level table (NUM_PROBES = [0,1,6,32,16,32,128,256,512,768,1500], greedy parsing at levels <= 3) searches less than zlib at level 9 (1500 probes vs zlib's max_chain 4096); level 6 settings match and the level-6 result is a tie, so the 1.11x-1.38x level-3/9 wins likely buy speed with compression ratio, and the README reports no compressed sizes. crabz -p 2 at level 9 runs more than twice as fast as its own -p 1 (19.977 s vs 44.907 s), which suggests the two tools count threads differently. The 'all Rust' backend still links the C mimalloc allocator. Numbers are from the Ubuntu 20 era with pigz 2.4, three runs each; the README itself says 'none of this is groundbreaking'. Plain-gzip decompression is single-threaded flate2 MultiGzDecoder over miniz_oxide against pigz -d.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated in the README. From the sources: compression runs gzp's parallel block pipeline over flate2's miniz_oxide backend, whose level presets do less match searching than zlib at levels 3 and 9 (level 6 presets match and tie pigz); decompression is miniz_oxide inflate via flate2 MultiGzDecoder against pigz's zlib-based inflate. No Rust-versus-C codegen mechanism is shown.

notes: All claimed numbers match the 'Flate2 rust backend' tables (level 3 1T 10.167 vs 11.338 s, 32T 0.547 vs 0.755; level 9 1T 44.907 vs 53.109, 32T 1.747 vs 2.086; level 6 tie; decompression 1.599-1.615 vs 1.696-1.767 s). Shortcomings to record: no compressed sizes while miniz_oxide's level 9 preset does far less search than zlib's (win likely trades ratio), README tables from an older benchmark.sh revision, rustc and pigz build flags unstated, C mimalloc linked as global allocator in the 'pure Rust' build. Not a duplicate: gzp and miniz_oxide are not in the catalog; pigz is (wave 9).

tier_reason: First-party hyperfine output in the README against macOS du -sh and diskus, with public source and tree generator (setup_benchmark.py), but no Mac model or CPU, no rustc version and no independent run, so C.

corrections.workload: Computing the total size of a synthetic tree built by setup_benchmark.py: 12 levels with branching factor two (4095 directories), 100 files of 70 bytes in every directory (409,500 files), warm disk cache. The README calls it '100 small files per level', but the script writes 100 files into each directory.
corrections.caveats: Synthetic tree and warm cache only (author says he found no reliable way to clear the macOS disk cache). Mac model not named. No LICENSE file and no license field in Cargo.toml. Not a language win: dumac runs a rayon work-stealing traversal on up to available_parallelism threads and reads name, type, inode and allocated size for a batch of entries per getattrlistbulk call, while BSD du walks single-threaded with fts and one stat per entry; dumac spends more total CPU (user+system 2.27 s vs du 1.43 s) to cut wall time. dumac counts only regular files and symlinks (directories' own blocks are not added) and dedups every inode, and its tests do not compare its output with du's. The author's first blog post (healeycodes.com, blocked here; search snippet only) reported 6.4x vs du and 2.58x vs diskus for an earlier tokio-based version, while the README shows 5.66x and 3.26x.
corrections.why_faster: README, source and blog snippet: parallel directory traversal (rayon, thread count capped at 224 file handles) plus the macOS getattrlistbulk syscall, which returns attributes for many entries per call instead of du's per-file stat (400k+ syscalls on this tree per the blog snippet). Syscall choice and parallelism, not codegen.

notes: Numbers match the README (563.1 ms vs du 3.186 s, 5.66x; vs diskus 1.834 s, 3.26x). Shortcomings to record: no license (reference only), Mac model unstated, warm cache only, win is parallelism plus getattrlistbulk rather than Rust, output equivalence with du not tested, earlier blog numbers differ (snippet only). Metadata checked: 65 stars, 19 commits, last commit 2025-08-07 (stale). diskus is already listed (wave 11); dumac is a separate project, not a duplicate.
